articles.title: Indian solar mission's new findings throw light on enduring Sun mysteries
articles.description:
By

Geeta Pandey

BBC Correspondent

,

Reporting from

Delhi

Published

34 minutes ago

One of the most enduring mysteries that has been puzzling scientists forever is how the Sun's outer atmosphere - the corona - is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. And how does the corona continue to remain so hot despite frequent eruptions during which it loses huge amounts of energy?

Astrophysicists in India now say the latest findings from

Aditya-L1

, the country's first solar observation mission in space, have provided them some vital clues to unlocking those mysteries. Their findings are revealed in a recent paper published in the prestigious Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The temperature variations in different regions of the Sun defy the laws of physics, says leading Indian solar astrophysicist Prof R Ramesh of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) who led the study.

If you cut through the Sun's layers, deep inside is the core where the temperature is 15 million Celsius. Travel outwards to the surface or the photosphere - the part that we see from the Earth - it's about 5,500C. Far away from the core is the Sun's outermost layer or corona where the temperature is about 2 million C - it can sometimes go up to 40 million C.

Prof Ramesh says the corona is where extreme weather events - such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) - originate, during which large amounts of energy is released by the Sun into space. The CMEs cause beautiful auroras, and they can also affect life on Earth by causing geomagnetic storms that can knock down power grids and affect weather and communication satellites.

In normal or low-activity times, the Sun launches two to three CMEs a day. During the maximum solar activity cycle that comes every 11 years, there can be 10 or more in a single day.

"Now if the Sun is losing such huge amounts of energy with each CME and it's not replenished, the star at the centre of our solar system would lose all its energy and Earth would plunge into an irreversible deep freeze," Prof Ramesh says.

But since that's not happening, it means there's a "mechanism" by which the corona is able to maintain its inexplicably high temperature, he says.

Scientists put it down to two factors - one, the bubbling boiling motions on the Sun's surface that constantly generate waves which, as they travel outwards, carry energy to the corona - a bit like sea waves carrying foam and froth to the shore.

The second is the "tangled magnetic field lines" in the Sun's atmosphere that constantly snap and then reconnect. Prof Ramesh says a CME occurs when these twisting, looping lines - which resemble braided hair - rupture, throwing out massive clouds of magnetised plasma and gas in space. They often originate near sunspots, which are darker, cooler spots on the Sun where magnetic fields are particularly strong.

"But then these lines reconnect and the Sun replenishes the lost energy back within hours," he adds.

Why 2026 will be a year like no other for India's Sun mission

How important are India's Moon mission findings?

Why it costs India so little to reach the Moon and Mars

In their paper, Prof Ramesh says they have been able to quantify how much energy each of the two systems supply to the corona – which explains both why it's so many times hotter to begin with and how it retains that temperature after consistently losing energy.

Their study, he says, clearly shows that it's the second system that supplies most of the energy.

"Though the waves generated as a result of the bubbling, boiling motions on the Sun's surface generate and transport energy, their contribution is very little - they supply only 7% of the energy requirement.

"The remaining 93% comes because the Sun reconfigures itself and replenishes the lost energy."

To arrive at that calculation, Prof Ramesh says they studied a "very energetic" CME that took place on 5 August 2024. Emissions were recorded by Aditya-L1's coronagraph called Velc (Visible Emission Line Coronagraph).

"We saw that in 10 hours after the CME, the tangled field lines were able to go back to their original place, they reconnected and corona's energy was reconfigured," he said.

Aditya-L1: India's Sun mission reaches final destination

Chandrayaan-3: India makes historic landing near Moon's south pole

"We do recognise that energy generated by bubbly motions plays a major role in it, but we have evidence that it is not sufficient. Our study shows that the magnetic field lines snapping and reconnecting everywhere on the Sun are the primary source for supplying most of the energy."

These data, Prof Ramesh says, "provide an important benchmark" for future studies into the potential energy generation mechanisms in the Sun's atmosphere.

"I think they would help answer the fundamental questions of physics that defy logic," he says.

articles.title: 'Two out of four, baby' - Hunt wins 200m as she eyes historic quadruple
articles.description:
By

Emily Salley

BBC Sport journalist

Published

13 August 2026

Britain's Amy Hunt charged to 200m glory to secure her second gold medal of the European Championships - but the sprinter has her sights set on a historic quadruple in Birmingham.

The 24-year-old wants to "be iconic" and become the first athlete to win four European gold medals in the same tournament.

And after triumphing in the 100m on Monday, she added another gold to her collection with a season's best time of 22.19 seconds in the 200m final on Thursday.

Hunt reeled in rival and compatriot Asher-Smith down the back straight to cross the line first.

"Two out of four, baby!" Hunt told BBC TV.

"This is becoming a magical week and one I will remember for the rest of my life."

Hunt is set to compete in the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events later and says there will be "no celebrations and no champagne until Sunday night".

"I have got a debt to the ladies," she said.

"We have got to come out here and make sure we show them who the best sprinting nation is in Europe."

Asher-Smith was beaten to silver by just 0.01 seconds by Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who set a new national record.

"It unfolded exactly how I thought it would," two-time European 200m silver medallist Nethaneel Mitchell-Blake said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I knew Dina would run a blistering bend and then say 'Amy, come and catch me'. And that's what Amy has done."

After struggling in the 200m earlier this summer, Hunt said she was ready for a "renewal of our vows" in the event.

And the Briton kept her promise with a composed performance that ended with her powering through the final 40m to beat her competitors and clinch gold.

"Amy was phenomenal. She came off that bend like a train," three-time world heptathlon champion Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill said on BBC TV.

"It was so exciting to see Dina and Amy side by side. Amy said she was going to do it - and she did."

Hunt held her arms aloft and pointed to the sky as she emulated Asher-Smith's 100m-200m European double in 2018.

"Amy has it all. The speed, the endurance, the confidence, and now the double," said former men's 1500m world champion Steve Cram.

"This is Amy's stage at the moment."

'Disappointed' Asher-Smith 'held on as hard as she could'

After getting off to a rapid start, Asher-Smith was unable to hold off Hunt and Adeleke in the final push, but in finishing third she claimed a ninth European medal - a tally only bettered by the 10 of Polish ex-sprinter Irena Szewinska.

"Dina was not handing it to Amy. She was going to make her work hard," former British 400m runner Allison Curbishley said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Asher-Smith held on as hard as she could. Then she started to over-stride, and the hips dropped."

After finishing fifth in Monday's 100m final, Asher-Smith returned for the 200m to continue her bid to win a historic seventh gold and become the joint-most successful athlete in the history of the championships.

But there was further disappointment for the 30-year-old, who won European 200m gold in 2016 and 2018.

"I'm disappointed to have a bronze, but I think 10 years after my first one it is such an achievement to be in a place to come back year after year," Asher-Smith told BBC TV.

"It doesn't matter what's going on in my life, just come and continue to be one of the fastest women in the world. Happy to have done that today."

Before the race, there were hopes of a British one-two-three on the podium, with Asher-Smith, Hunt and Eduan holding the three fastest times in Europe this year.

However, Eduan - who beat Hunt to win her first British title in June - finished sixth.

But Hunt's second sprint gold continues Britain's dominance in the sprint events in Birmingham after Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu secured a one-two finish in the men's 100m, while Matthew Hudson-Smith stormed to 400m victory on Wednesday.

articles.title: English makes history with European 800m gold
articles.description:
By

Andy Gray

BBC Sport NI Journalist

Published

47 minutes ago

Mark English has become the first man to win a gold medal for Ireland at the European Athletics Championships after he won the 800m in Birmingham.

English moved into first place inside the final 100 metres as he surged past Croatia's Marino Bloudek to win with a time of 1:45.26.

Ben Pattison was sixth, while there was disappointment for his Great Britain team-mate Max Burgin, who was forced to withdraw from the final after he picked up an injury in the warm-up.

But the night belonged to English, who finally won European gold after his bronze medals from 2014 in Zurich and four years ago in Munich.

The 33-year-old was the favourite for gold after he broke Olaf Beyer's 48-year European record in his semi-final at the Alexander Stadium.

And while he did not lead the final until he passed the hard-charging Bloudek turning on to the home straight, he delivered in style and fell to his knees as he crossed the line.

The gold for the Donegal runner, who is a qualified doctor, was the first medal of the Championships for Ireland before Rhasidat Adeleke claimed women's 200m silver in the following race.

Hunt surges to 200m glory to win second European gold

Published

11 minutes ago

English won his first European medal - a bronze - as a 21-year-old in 2014, and was third in Munich in 2022.

"It's just relief. I have been trying for a lifetime to get a title," English told BBC Sport.

"It was relief in 2014 when I got my first medal and relief today as well. It is just amazing.

"I have made a few changes, moved to a new coach [Justin Rinaldi] and he has been amazing. Amazing in terms of advice before races. I have to give big praise to him."

Bloudek of Croatia held on to win silver and Spain's Mohamed Attaoui claimed bronze.

Pattison, the sole British runner after the injury to Burgin, was in a strong position heading into the final 100m but fell short of a medal.

"I'm gutted. It was a great opportunity today to add to my medal collection," Pattison said.

"I gave myself too much work to do, and the legs weren't there. I'm just disappointed."

Adeleke wins silver behind Hunt

In the race after English's historic win, Ireland won their second medal of the night as Adeleke took silver in the women's 200m behind home favourite Amy Hunt.

After an injury-plagued year, Adeleke only returned to action at the Irish National Championships in the build-up to Birmingham.

The 23-year-old made a strong start and put in a late charge, and while Hunt was clear out front, Adeleke was able to pip Dina Asher-Smith on the line by just 0.01 seconds, in a time of 22.28 - a new Irish record.

It is a fourth European medal for Adeleke, who claimed a silver in the 400m in Rome two years ago.

She also won gold in the mixed 4x400m relay and a silver in the women's relay at the same Championships.

Later that year she finished fourth at the Paris Olympics in the 400m but, after an injury-hit two years since, it marks a return to form as she returned to the European podium.

With Commonwealth Games champion Kate O'Connor to come in the heptathlon, against the returning Katarina Johnson-Thompson, there are hopes the Irish medal rush has not finished yet.

articles.title: Why Elite Ultrarunners Fall So Often Late in a Race, and What It Reveals About Every Runner's Body
articles.description:
When Ben Dhiman won the 2026 UTMB in 18:16:29, becoming the first man ever to break 19 hours at the race, he did it after falling hard with roughly 10 kilometres to go.
He got up, kept running, and still won by more than 31 minutes.
The fall was not bad luck. It was physics.
Elite runners fall late in long races for the same reasons recreational runners injure themselves on Sunday long runs.

The Actual Data On What Fatigue Does To A Runner

A 2016 study on a 110-kilometre mountain ultramarathon measured neuromuscular fatigue and biomechanics before and after the race.
Runners showed maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) decrements of roughly 35 percent for the knee extensors and 28 percent for the plantar flexors after the race.
That means the muscles that control landing and push-off had lost about a third of their peak force capacity.
Step frequency increased by roughly 2.7 percent as a compensatory response. Ankle range of motion decreased by around 4.1 percent.
The runners were, in effect, shuffling more than running by the end.

Why Their Bodies Chose That Strategy

The change in foot strike was fatigue-dependent, not random.
Runners who started as rearfoot strikers landed less on the heel by the end. Runners who started as forefoot strikers landed flatter.
Both groups converged on a landing pattern that minimised impact shock and muscle stretch.
It was, per the researchers, a protective adjustment.

The Postural Stability Collapse

The other reason elite runners fall late in ultras has nothing to do with muscle force.
It has to do with the sensory system that tells the brain where the body is in space.
A separate study on an 80-kilometre mountain race measured runners' postural stability with a force platform, before and after the race.
The centre-of-pressure length increased by 36 percent in the front-to-back direction and 29 percent in the side-to-side direction after the race.
In plain English: they could no longer stand still without swaying more than a third further than they had that morning.
Now translate that onto a technical descent at 10 kilometres from a UTMB finish, in the dark, on wet rocks. A fall is the expected outcome.

The Signal Recreational Runners Should Actually Take From This

Falls in long races are not a discipline problem or an attention problem.
They are the visible tip of a physiological cascade that begins hours earlier.
Every long training run does a smaller version of the same thing to a recreational body. Muscles lose force, proprioception dulls, landing changes.

What Elites Do About It, In Race

Ben Dhiman fell, got up, and finished.
Elites recover in-race for one specific reason.
Their aerobic base is deep enough that the metabolic cost of the fall itself is negligible against their remaining energy budget.
A recreational runner falling at the same relative point in a race has a much smaller cushion.
Which is why the actionable lesson is not "be more careful late".
It is "train the fatigue-resistance the elites take for granted".

The Two Training Adaptations That Matter Most

The first is single-leg strength work.
Runners who add split squats, step-downs, and single-leg deadlifts to their week show measurable improvements in late-race MVC retention.
The second is deliberate pre-fatigued balance training.
Standing on one leg with eyes closed for 30 seconds after a hard run is uncomfortable and revealing.
It also trains the same proprioceptive system that collapses in a 20-hour race.

The Injury Connection Runners Miss

The most common weekend runner injuries all cluster around the tissues that fatigue-related biomechanical changes overload.
Runner's knee tracks with quadriceps force loss and altered landing. Plantar fasciitis tracks with ankle stiffness and reduced range of motion.
The mechanism that makes an elite fall at kilometre 164 is the mechanism that gives a recreational runner a strained calf at kilometre 26.
Our full breakdown of the most common knee injuries in runners covers the front-of-knee mechanisms in detail.
And our practical exercise guide to preventing runner's knee translates the strength-work findings into a home routine.

The Trail Super-Shoe Complication

A 2025 review on ultramarathon footwear noted that current-generation trail super-shoes degrade under racing conditions.
Their functional properties change during the event itself.
Which means a shoe optimised for kilometre 50 may not be the shoe underfoot at kilometre 150. We covered how this is reshaping ultra results in our piece on
trail super-shoes rewriting who wins ultras.

What The Fall Actually Meant For Dhiman

Dhiman told reporters at the finish that the fall did not surprise him.
The surprise was that his body still had another 10 kilometres in it at that pace.
That, more than the winning time or the 45-minute margin, is the training story of his year.
It is also what separates a training block that leads to a UTMB win from one that leads to a DNF at Grand Col Ferret.
The peer-reviewed data on late-race biomechanics is available in the 110km ultramarathon fatigue study on PMC.

articles.title: Eight Months Pregnant and Still Sub-3. Ali Anderson Runs 2:59 in Sydney
articles.description:
Ali Anderson ran 2:59:43 at the Sydney Marathon on Sunday.
She is 29, from Oklahoma, and she was 32 weeks pregnant when she crossed the line.
That time puts her inside the roughly 1 percent of women who break three hours for the marathon distance.
She ran it with seventeen seconds to spare.
It was her second marathon of the pregnancy. At Boston in April, at 13 weeks, she ran a 2:41:58 personal best and announced the news afterward.

The arc from Boston to Sydney

Sydney was Anderson's seventh marathon overall and her fourth World Marathon Major. She entered before she knew she was pregnant.
Sydney's race organizers offered her a way out.
Their 2026 pregnancy and postpartum policy let a pregnant entrant defer her spot to 2027, 2028, or 2029 on a doctor's letter.
The deadline passed at 5pm AEST on August 14. She let it slide.
She told News24 Australia she saw no reason to give up the start. She joined a record 40,000 entrants running from North Sydney to the Opera House.
The pace math is worth pausing on. A sub-3 marathon requires roughly 6:51 per mile.
Anderson held that pace and little more, running about 41 seconds per mile slower than her Boston best.
She has said this is the last marathon before the birth. In her words, "I have put her through two marathons now and that is enough for her."

What the ACOG guidelines actually permit

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists updated its guidance in 2020, and it is more permissive than most people assume.
Vigorous-intensity exercise into the third trimester appears to be safe for most healthy pregnancies, according to the ACOG committee opinion. That includes running.
The guidelines also acknowledge that competitive athletes are a distinct category.
Elite athletes, defined loosely as women who train year-round at a high level, tend to maintain more strenuous training and resume high-intensity work sooner postpartum than the general population.

The caveats every pregnant runner should know

ACOG names four specific concerns for competitive athletes during pregnancy: avoiding hyperthermia, maintaining hydration, sustaining calorie intake to prevent weight loss, and staying under close medical supervision.
There is one intensity ceiling the research keeps returning to. Fetal heart rate decelerations have been reported when maternal effort exceeds roughly 90 percent of max heart rate.
Anderson's Sydney pace was under her own limit by design. She left seventeen seconds of buffer, not seventeen minutes.

What actually happens to the running body in the third trimester

Three physiological shifts define third-trimester running.
Center of gravity moves forward as the bump grows, and joint laxity increases as relaxin peaks.
The energy cost of running rises by roughly 10 to 15 percent.
None of that is dangerous, but all of it changes the effort-to-pace ratio.
That is the mechanical explanation for Anderson's roughly six-minute drop from Boston to Sydney. It was not fitness loss, it was carrying more, in a differently shaped frame, in warmer air.

What a study of 60 elite and recreational athletes actually found

A recent descriptive study followed 60 women who exercised through pregnancy above the standard guidelines. Ten were elite athletes averaging 11.6 hours of training per week, and 50 were recreational athletes at 7.0 hours per week.
Most resumed exercise within six weeks postpartum.
Most had spontaneous onset of labor and vaginal deliveries at term.
The mean birthweight was 3,487 grams, which is inside the normal healthy range.
Two of the elite athletes were diagnosed with gestational diabetes and two with hypertension during pregnancy.
None of the 50 recreational athletes reported any pregnancy complications. The full paper is available on PMC for anyone who wants the primary data.

The course she ran on

The Sydney Marathon course is not gentle. It carries 313 meters of climbing against a net drop of 83 meters, which converts to roughly 1,027 feet up and 272 feet down.
That is more vertical than most World Marathon Majors offer.
Anderson also ran it in her seventh marathon start, on a body carrying an extra 20 or so pounds of gestational weight.
A closer look at what the course actually demands sits in this breakdown of why Sydney is now the hardest of the World Marathon Majors.

What she is not claiming, and what she is

Anderson is not claiming pregnant women should race marathons.
She is not a physiologist and her interviews have been careful.
What she is doing is quieter. She is showing that the assumption of complete rest through pregnancy, still the default advice most women get, is not what the current medical guidelines actually say for someone who was already training at a high level going in.
She had a third marathon booked for December and had planned an attempt at the American Olympic Marathon Trials standard. USATF has set that at 2:37:00 for women in 2028.
Her Boston time sits 4 minutes and 58 seconds outside it.
She has time.

The wider category she now belongs in

Anderson is not the first athlete to race deep into a pregnancy, and she will not be the last.
The precedents span every distance from track to ultra.
What makes her case land differently is the specificity of the numbers: a 2:59:43 at 32 weeks, five months after a 2:41:58 personal best at 13 weeks.
That is a training log, not an anecdote.
She joins a small but growing catalog of runners who have stayed inside their own effort envelope while their body changed around them
It is the same envelope, on a different scale, that shapes what happens to running after 40, or what a marathon looks like at 90.

The finish line she actually crossed

The clock in the Sydney Opera House forecourt read 2:59:43 as Anderson came through.
She had entered the race before she knew she was pregnant.
She raced it anyway, stayed inside the guidelines she was working with, and left the door open on a Trials standard she has almost three years to chase.
Seventeen seconds under three hours, at 32 weeks, on a course most people find punishing sober.
That is the story, and the story does not require any interpretation to land.

articles.title: Julien Veysseyre Crossed the UTMB Finish Line on One Leg and Made History
articles.description:
Picture from HOKA UTMB Mont Blanc
Shortly after 4 p.m. on Sunday, Julien Veysseyre walked under the finish arch in Chamonix with his children beside him and became the first amputee ever to finish the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc.
Official timing places the 39-year-old Frenchman 1,475th in 44 hours, 16 minutes, 4 seconds, on the 173.6km loop with about 9,700 meters of climbing.

What The 44 Hours Actually Cost Him

Veysseyre lost his right leg to a workplace accident at 18.
He came to trail running through triathlon, where he was crowned world para-triathlon champion in 2023, before Salomon brought him onto its para team.
Last year he finished the CCC, the 100km sister race to UTMB. This year he came for the main event.
A below-knee amputee uses roughly 10 to 30 percent more metabolic energy to walk than a runner with two biological legs, per a 2018 paper in Scientific Reports.
Running on a blade adds socket friction. It loads the sound side harder, and it changes gait on every technical step.
Now stretch that penalty across 174 kilometers of alpine trail and roughly two full nights of movement.

Five Guides. Two Prosthetics. One Route.

Veysseyre did not go alone.
Five pacers rotated through the two nights on the mountain. Part of what they carried was a
second prosthesis, swapped in as the terrain changed, according to AFP.
La Montagne tracked his stops and counted just 1 hour, 59 minutes, 16 seconds off his feet across the entire race.
That included two longer breaks of 37 and 40 minutes, one on each night.
The rest of it was motion.

The Course Itself Was Not The One Runners Signed Up For

UTMB organizers pushed the start two hours late on Friday, from 5:45 p.m. to 7:45 p.m., over a thunderstorm risk on the ridge line.
They also cut the Pyramides Calcaires section out of the route, shortening the loop and adjusting the final cutoff to 6:30 p.m. on Sunday.
Veysseyre reached that finish arch with roughly 2 hours, 25 minutes of cutoff time still on the clock.
Race winner Ben Dhiman had been done for a full day by then, breaking 19 hours in the process.
You can look up the full winning story of the 2026 field in our coverage of Kilian Jornet's return campaign and the men's field.
Pictures from HOKA UTMB Mont Blanc

Why This Result Sits Outside The Official Rankings

UTMB does not run a para classification.
That means Veysseyre's name appears in the standard M4 (35-39) men's category, mixed in with every non-amputee runner in his age group.
There is no adjusted time, no separate podium, no asterisk in the results file.
The result is a plain finish, ranked against every other finisher.
Which, given what covering that ground actually costs a single-leg athlete, is the point.

The Field Was Not A Small One

Roughly 2,400 runners left the Place du Triangle de l'Amitié on Friday evening.
Many of the biggest names in the sport were not among them. We laid out the headline absences from the 2026 UTMB elite field earlier this year.
Their absence did not shrink what Veysseyre did. If anything, the story that walked under the arch on Sunday afternoon was the story of the weekend.

The Champagne In The Prosthesis

One image made the rounds in French sports coverage on Sunday night.
Veysseyre poured champagne into his racing blade at the finish and drank from it in front of his crew.
The gesture was small. The subtext was the point.
A device that once defined what he had lost was, on Sunday, the thing he was celebrating from.

What Comes Next For Him

Veysseyre has said the UTMB was the biggest challenge he would ever attempt.
He described the finish, in mixed zone, in the language of someone still trying to believe it.
The scale of the reception surprised him. By his own account, most of the runners still out on the mountain knew his first name.
A single UTMB result does not create a para category on its own.
It does, however, make one harder to argue against.
Every future amputee entrant now has an actual finish to point at, in an actual results file, with an actual bib number.
The ceiling moved on Sunday afternoon. Somebody had to move it first.
Veysseyre had spent three years preparing for a single objective.
He had built through the para-triathlon world title and the CCC 100km as staging posts, not as end points.
Whether he returns to the Chamonix start line is an open question. Whether other amputee entrants will now line up behind him is not.
The full context of the run, including guide rotations and split analysis, is documented in Marathon Handbook's finish-line report.
The metabolic-cost figure comes from an open-access study on lower-limb amputee locomotion hosted on PMC.

articles.title: At 90, a Retired Doctor Just Became the Oldest Person Ever to Climb Kilimanjaro
articles.description:
Courtesy World Wide Trekking

His name is Dr. Art Ulene, and the walk lasted 15 days.
At the top, standing at roughly 19,341 feet, he ate birthday cake. Then he danced.
That summit made him the oldest human known to have climbed the highest mountain in Africa.

The record he broke, and the one he was chasing

The prior record belonged to Anne Lorimor, an American who summited Kilimanjaro in July 2019 at 89 years and 37 days.
The Lorimor record was officially recognised by Guinness. The Ulene claim, at 90 years exactly, awaits Guinness verification.
That verification typically takes up to three months, per Guinness policy. The National Park Service reportedly had a representative on the mountain to witness the summit.
According to reporting by Alaska News Source, the ascent was confirmed the same day by his daughter, Dr. Valerie Ulene.

Who Dr. Art Ulene actually is

Ulene is a retired OB-GYN. He is also, for a certain generation of American viewers, a familiar television face.
He served for years as the medical correspondent on the NBC TODAY show, translating clinical research into practical advice for a huge audience.
That professional background is not decorative. It is the entire reason he framed this climb the way he did.

The frame he keeps using in every interview

In a conversation with NPR before the trip, Ulene laid out the sentence every runner and every ageing athlete should copy down.
Most people, he said, worry about their lifespan. Smart people worry about their healthspan, which is how many of those years are spent in good health.
His stated ambition is for the two numbers to be equal, meaning he wants to be in the best possible health right up to the last day.
Kilimanjaro was the loudest way he could think of to make that argument in public.
Courtesy of CareScout

The climb itself, in his own words

This was not a heroic sprint up the mountain.
The full trip took 15 days.
Eleven and a half of those were spent going up. Four were spent coming down.
The group carried a folding chair for him. Roughly every hour, they set it up and he sat for five to 10 minutes to recover.
He told The Spokesman-Review that his legs simply would not go any faster and that pace, not fitness, was the ceiling.

The hardest part was not what most people assume

Ulene has said the hardest part of the climb was not the altitude or the cold.
It was lifting himself over large rocks on the technical sections. The descent was almost as tough, because a 90-year-old body has to actively brake every step to avoid tumbling.
His summit line, remembered afterwards, is the one worth repeating. He kept telling himself that all he had to do was put one foot in front of the other.
That is not a motivational poster. That is the mechanical reality of ultra-endurance at any age.

This was not his first Kilimanjaro

Ulene had climbed the mountain twice before.
The first time was in 2011, at 75, with his wife Priscilla. She was 72.
He attempted it again in a subsequent year and turned back before the summit. That returned attempt is why the 90th-birthday climb was not a first-time act, but a settled score.
The relevant lesson for older runners is quiet but important.
Attempts that end short of the goal are not failures. They are altitude acclimatisation for the future.

Why this belongs on a running website

Ulene is not a distance runner in any formal sense. He is a doctor, a skier, and now a record-holding climber.
The reason his story matters here is that he is a living illustration of the same principle that drives every late-life running profile on the site.
The runners who keep going into their 80s and 90s share the same governing idea. Ulene just chose a mountain to say it out loud.

The company he is now in

At 90, Ulene joins a small, extraordinary cohort. The site has covered a few of its other members.
There is Mike Fremont, who ran a 6-hour 35-minute marathon at 90, and there is Emma Maria Mazzenga, who broke the over-90 200-metre world record.
Every one of them is running the same experiment Ulene ran. Push the ceiling of what an older body can do, and watch it move.

What actually let a 90-year-old climb this mountain

There is a temptation to file this under "special genetics" and move on. That is not what the evidence shows.
The list Ulene keeps naming is closer to the standard longevity checklist than most journalists let on.
  •  Decades of consistent aerobic base. He skied, hiked, and stayed active without long dormant stretches.
  •  A functional obsession with health, not a wellness aesthetic. As a doctor, he tracked the numbers most people ignore.
  •  Deliberate goal-setting into old age. The Kilimanjaro attempt at 90 was announced in advance, in public.
  •  Pacing over pride. The chair-every-hour strategy is the reason he summited when a younger, faster ego would have blown up at 15,000 feet.

The pattern the running literature keeps confirming

The science on running counteracting the effects of aging points at the same mechanism. Sustained aerobic loading protects cardiovascular capacity, bone density, and mitochondrial function far past the point most people assume.
Ulene did not run 26.2 miles at 90. He did something arguably harder over 15 days.
The underlying physiology is close to identical. Cardiovascular economy, muscular durability, and stubbornness.

What is next for a 90-year-old record holder

The answer, unsurprisingly, is not retirement.
Ulene has already bought a season ski pass at Deer Valley in Utah. He plans to take lessons from an 80-year-old instructor.
He has also said he wants to keep inspiring people to live as well as they can at any age, while carefully noting he is not telling every older person to climb Kilimanjaro.
The offer he is actually making is smaller and more useful. Pick a big enough goal that it forces the daily choices, and the daily choices will do the rest.

The line from the summit worth stealing

Asked how someone climbs Kilimanjaro at 90, Ulene gave the answer that every runner already knows.
One step at a time. That is the mechanical answer, the philosophical answer, and the training answer, all in the same sentence.
Ulene is 90. He has already announced he is going down mountains next, on skis.
The healthspan-equals-lifespan idea used to sound like marketing. On July 13, 2026, a retired OB-GYN turned it into a Guinness application at 19,341 feet.

articles.title: Mark Dowdle Just Ran for 94 Straight Hours Without Sleep to Win the Last Soul Ultra
articles.description:
The Last Soul Ultra does not have a finish line in the usual sense.
It has a 4.17-mile loop, a bell that rings every hour on the hour, and one rule.
Complete the loop inside the hour, or you are out. The race ends only when a single runner remains.
This year that runner was Mark Dowdle, a 29-year-old American, and he stayed on the course for 94 straight hours.

What Actually Happened Near Düsseldorf

The 2026 Last Soul Ultra started on Friday, August 14, at a former military base in Germany.
169 athletes lined up. Four days later, only two were left running.
Dowdle was in a duel with 27-year-old Ayyoub "Ello" El Osrouti of Germany, who had also been the last runner-up at the inaugural 2025 edition of the race.
On the 94th yard, El Osrouti could not continue.
He walked most of the previous loop, tried to run once more, and finally lay down in a wheat field beside the course. Dowdle completed his final solo lap, the way backyard-format ultras always end, and became the Last Soul Standing.

The numbers behind the win

The official Ultramarathon Database record lists Dowdle at 94 completed yards, which works out to roughly 629.8 kilometres, or the equivalent of about 15 marathons back to back with no sleep.
For context, no backyard ultra on German soil had ever crossed the 90-yard mark before Sunday morning of this race.
Dowdle and El Osrouti crossed it together on the fourth night.

How Dowdle Almost Missed the Start Line

The story that has travelled the fastest is the one about his flights.
Dowdle had a work commitment on the Thursday before the Friday start, and his flights out of the United States fell apart.
According to reporting from BroBible and the race broadcast, a private jet was chartered to get him to Germany, and he arrived at the venue with about 15 minutes to spare before the first bell.
He had never been to Germany before.
His previous backyard best was 73 loops, set at Nick Bare's BPN Go One More ultra in Texas in April, where he beat Kim Gottwald and Harvey Lewis.
He beat that mark on Sunday night at Last Soul with days still to go.

Backyard-format ultras, explained

The backyard format was invented by Lazarus Lake, the same organiser behind the Barkley Marathons.
Every runner starts together at the top of the hour, covers the same 4.166-mile loop, and returns to base camp for whatever time is left in that hour.
Rest, eat, use the toilet, sleep for a few minutes if you can.
Then the bell rings again, and you go back out.
You do not have to run fast.
You have to keep coming back.
That is a very different problem from a road marathon, which is why we broke down why durability, not speed, is the real weapon in ultramarathons.

What This Race Says About Where Ultrarunning Is Going

The Last Soul Ultra started in 2025 as a niche event with a runner-turned-YouTuber named Kim Gottwald as its founder.
This year, its livestream pulled more than 100,000 concurrent viewers on YouTube on the final night.
That is a scale of audience nobody has associated with the backyard format before.
It also raises the sport's profile in a way that pulls in crossover athletes.
Dowdle himself did not come from endurance running.
He was a college football and lacrosse player in Illinois before switching disciplines.
That background is starting to look less like a curiosity in ultras and more like a pattern.

The mental piece

Ultrarunners talk about the first 24 hours of a backyard event as the hardest section, and Dowdle has said the same.
After the first day, in his framing, you have already rewritten the task in your brain.
The loop is now something you have already done many times, and the next one is just another instance of a thing you know you can complete.
That kind of framing is how Sally McRae kept going through hallucinations and eight hours of vomiting at a 200-mile race, and it shows up again and again in athletes who last at these distances.

The Wider Backyard Boom

Kenyan and Kalenjin dominance still defines the marathon.
But the endurance world beyond the marathon is being reshaped by athletes like Sophie Power, who broke the 48-hour treadmill world record, and Max Jolliffe, who ran the fastest Badwater 135 in history this summer.
The peaks in these formats are getting higher because more athletes are willing to attack them.
Dowdle's 94 yards is not the world record.
The all-time backyard world best now sits well past 100 loops.
But it is the deepest performance the format has seen on German soil, it happened live in front of a huge international audience, and it was won by a runner who was still moving well when his rival stopped.

The Question He Asked Himself Every Hour

Near the end, Dowdle posted a video from the course.
He said he and his crew had been asking one question over and over as he came back into base camp. Is the job finished?
Every hour, for four days, the answer was no. Then it was yes, and he sat down.
The Last Soul Ultra now moves into planning for 2027.
Whatever it does next, it has its first breakout champion, and he did it on 15 minutes' notice and no sleep.

articles.title: At Cocodona 250, She Beat Every Man In The Field. Now She Races Courtney Dauwalter At UTMB.
articles.description:
Photo Credit : @scottrokisphoto | @howiesternphoto | @_anastasiawilde

When Rachel Entrekin crossed the finish line at the Cocodona 250 in May, she had just done something no woman had ever done in the race’s history.
She had run 254 miles across the Arizona desert in 56 hours, 9 minutes and 48 seconds, beating every man in the field and taking almost eight hours off her own women’s course record.
The men’s previous course record, set by Kilian Korth, went with it.
On Friday 28 August, she runs her first UTMB, against Ruth Croft and Courtney Dauwalter.

Who is Rachel Entrekin?

Entrekin is 34, born in Madison, Alabama, and lives in Conifer, Colorado.
She has a doctorate in physical therapy and used to work at an oncology rehabilitation centre before turning full-time to running.
She did not compete in any sport at school.
Her own explanation, quoted in her hometown paper, is that she started running while pursuing an undergraduate degree at the University of Alabama and did not stop.

The credentials nobody was watching

Before her breakout Cocodona 250 win in May, most casual trail fans did not know her name.
They should have. In 2025 alone she won the Cocodona 250 (women’s), the High Lonesome 100 (with a course record), the Whiskey Basin 88K, the Pass Mountain 50 and the Aspen Backcountry Marathon, and finished second overall at the Mammoth 200.
She was named fourth in the 2025 UltraRunner of the Year vote, an extraordinary result for a runner who was still classed as “unknown” in mainstream previews.
She holds 15 fastest known times on established Sierra Nevada routes.
She lives in her car for weeks at a time between races.

What she did at Cocodona 250, in numbers

Cocodona 250 is a 407-kilometre point-to-point across the Arizona desert with more than 38,000 feet of climbing and extreme temperature swings.
Entrekin ran it in 56:09:48 and slept a total of 19 minutes, split across three short naps of under 10 minutes each.
Her average moving pace, including those stops, worked out to a 13:20 mile across three days on desert singletrack.
She beat Kilian Korth’s previous men’s course record by more than an hour and became the first woman to win the race outright in its history.
The nearest historical comparison for that kind of overall win is Courtney Dauwalter’s 2017 Moab 240, when she beat the field by 10 hours. Entrekin is now in that conversation.

How she got the UTMB start line

Auto-entry, not the lottery.
In March 2026 she took third woman and 14th overall at the Chianti Ultra Trail 120K, one of the UTMB World Series races that offers a guaranteed elite entry.
The race itself is a preview of everything that will happen on Friday. Dauwalter passed Entrekin with less than nine miles to run, and Entrekin’s post-race description captured the moment better than any journalist could: “I am hauling ass, she is just hauling better ass.”
Dauwalter has now faced Entrekin at Chianti and at Cocodona 250. UTMB is round three of the season.

The problem: UTMB is not Cocodona

Every UTMB rookie faces the same wall.
The 174-kilometre loop around Mont-Blanc has 9,900 metres of vertical gain packed into a single stage, most of it above 1,800 metres, most of it on technical singletrack, and a substantial portion of it run in the dark.
It is not a 250-mile desert race with sleep stops.
It is a compressed, high-altitude, weather-exposed climb-and-descent race that punishes fast starts and rewards climbers with quick recovery.
History is against her. According to the 2026 UTMB women’s preview from iRunFar, the last UTMB rookie to win the women’s race was Courtney Dauwalter in 2019.
That is one first-time winner in six years, and it happened to be one of the greatest ultrarunners of the modern era.

What is in her favour

The physiology is there.
Cocodona rewards the same durability that UTMB does, and Entrekin has more of it than almost anyone in the field.
She has spent 2025 and 2026 training almost exclusively on high-altitude terrain, stacking weeks of 100 to 110 miles with 20,000 to 25,000 feet of climbing.
Her fuelling is a known strength.
She works with a dedicated nutrition coach and has crewed for enough Alps races that she understands what UTMB aid stations do and do not carry.

What to watch for on Friday and Saturday

Watch the first climb up to Le Delevret. If Entrekin is in the front pack there, she has decided to race with Croft and Dauwalter rather than run her own splits.
Watch the descent into Courmayeur, around kilometre 80.
That is where the wheels came off for Courtney Dauwalter in 2025, and it is where every projection has Entrekin either committing to a top-five finish or slipping into a survival race.
And watch the last climb out of Vallorcine, around kilometre 150.
Trail super shoes are rewriting who wins ultras, and that final descent into Chamonix is where the fresh legs eat the field.

The bigger story

Whatever happens on Friday night into Saturday afternoon, Entrekin’s UTMB debut is the most significant expansion of the women’s elite field since Katie Schide arrived in 2023.
She is the answer to a question the sport had stopped asking.
What happens when a 250-mile runner comes down to 100 miles?
She is running against Ruth Croft, the only woman to have won all three UTMB World Series Finals races.
She is running against Courtney Dauwalter, three-time UTMB champion and the current UTMB Index leader at 859.
And she is running her first UTMB. Never even started one before.
The 100-mile UTMB starts on Friday 28 August at 17:45 CEST from Chamonix.
The official UTMB Mont-Blanc site has full tracking, and the 10 European ultra-running events you cannot miss guide has the rest of the calendar worth watching this season.
Rachel Entrekin has spent five years quietly building the deepest ultra-running résumé nobody was paying attention to. That stops this weekend.

articles.title: UTMB Is Making Runners Use Red Headlamps Through One Section This Year. Wildlife Is The Reason
articles.description:
Every runner heading to the start line of UTMB 2026 this Friday will be carrying a piece of kit they did not need before.
The rule is simple.
Two headlamps are mandatory, as they always have been, but for 2026 one of them must have a red-light mode, and inside the Réserve naturelle des Contamines-Montjoie that is the setting runners are required to use.
UTMB has cited the reserve’s nocturnal wildlife as the reason.
That single line hides a much larger conversation that has been building in Chamonix all summer.

What the rule actually says

The Réserve naturelle des Contamines-Montjoie sits on the French side of the Mont-Blanc massif and is one of the highest-altitude nature reserves in the Alps.
UTMB’s official race page for the 100-mile event lists the change under mandatory equipment: “one of your two headlamps must have a red-light mode.”
Runners are expected to switch to red light for the full duration of their transit through the reserve, which the flagship UTMB race enters within the first 40 kilometres from Chamonix.
The rule applies to the UTMB (100 miles), the CCC (100K) and the TDS, all three of which cross the reserve at some point.

Why red light matters for wildlife

White headlamp light disrupts nocturnal animals far more than red light does. Most mammals and birds cannot see red wavelengths well, so a red beam registers as much dimmer than a white one of the same brightness.
For the reserve, that matters. The area hosts ibex, chamois, marmots, ptarmigan and several bat species, all of which are active at night during summer.
Ten thousand runners passing through with white headlamps over 48 hours is not the same as one hiker with a torch. The cumulative light pollution is what UTMB is trying to reduce.

This is not the only change for 2026

The red headlamp rule is the most visible new requirement, but it is one of several.

Doping controls have doubled

UTMB has doubled the number of doping controls for race week, and for the first time those controls will extend to age-group entrants rather than only the elite fields.
The move follows a season in which the sport has been repeatedly asked whether its non-elite categories are subject to the same standards as its podium contenders.
For most amateur runners, the practical takeaway is simple. Any therapeutic use exemption should be filed and any supplement should be checked, because the tests are no longer limited to the front of the race.

The course has been reworked between Chamonix and Les Houches

The opening section from Chamonix to Les Houches has been reworked for 2026, which is why the published distance shifts slightly from previous editions.
For most runners the change is cosmetic.
For those with detailed split targets from previous years it matters, because the first 15 kilometres will not match old pace charts.

The vendor expo has been pulled back to Place du Mont-Blanc

François-Xavier Laffin, the new mayor of Chamonix who took office in March, has spent the summer laying out what he wants changed about UTMB week.
One of his interventions has already landed.
The vendor expo is confined to Place du Mont-Blanc from this year onwards, a smaller footprint than the sprawl of previous editions.
Laffin has also publicly called for fewer competitors crossing protected ground at night and a limit on how many supporters travel with each runner.
Neither has been formalised for 2026, but both are pressure points for the 2027 edition.

What this means if you are running

Two practical points before Friday.
Check your headlamps now. Most modern trail headlamps include a red mode, but not all of them make it easy to switch to under fatigue, and a fumbled toggle at 2am on a technical descent is not a memory anyone wants.
Practice the switch in training. Turn a red beam on and off in the dark, on rough ground, wearing gloves.
If your primary headlamp does not have red mode, either buy a second one that does or move a compliant lamp into the primary slot before Friday.
The best headlamps for runners guide has the models that meet the requirement and hold up to a full alpine night.

What this means if you are watching

You are watching the sport quietly shift into a new phase, one that trades the raw growth of the last decade for a tighter footprint on the terrain it races across.
The doping controls extending to age-group entrants is the more consequential rule change.
It signals that UTMB now sees itself as accountable for the full field, not just the elites the cameras follow.
The red headlamp rule is smaller, but it is the one that reveals the direction of travel.
Ultra-races have crossed protected land for years without significant restrictions, and that free pass is ending.

The wider picture

Chamonix hosts one of the busiest race weeks in world sport.
Ten thousand runners, roughly 60 per cent of them travelling from outside France, plus crews, plus supporters, plus media, plus a vendor village.
What the valley can absorb is now the animating question of every rule change UTMB makes. Speaking to L’Équipe over the summer, Laffin framed it as a question of what the mountains can carry, and what the town can carry.
The red headlamp rule is the answer nobody would have written down a decade ago, and it is the answer that will define how this race looks in a decade’s time.
Expect more of it.
The mandatory kit list, the doping regime, the vendor footprint and the night-crossing rules are all now in play, and every one of them will keep tightening.
That is the trade-off UTMB has accepted to keep racing where it races.
The alternative is to move the course, and nobody in Chamonix wants that.
For a broader take on how European ultra events are evolving under similar pressure, 10 European ultra-running events you cannot miss walks through the calendar and what each race is trying to protect.
The 100-mile UTMB starts on Friday 28 August at 17:45 CEST from Chamonix. Bring the red headlamp.

articles.title: Four Of Trail Running’s Biggest Names Are Missing From UTMB 2026. Here Is Why.
articles.description:
Pictures From Ian Corless, The Denver Post, Jeff Pachoud, Getty Images
The 2026 HOKA UTMB Mont-Blanc start list is one of the deepest in the race’s history, with 846 elite entrants across the week from 54 nationalities.
It is also one of the most conspicuous, because of who is not on it.
Four of the sport’s biggest names are out. Kilian Jornet, Jim Walmsley, defending men’s champion Tom Evans and course-record holder Katie Schide will all miss the 174-kilometre loop around Mont-Blanc on Friday 28 August.
Four different reasons, four different stories, and one race that suddenly looks very different from the one everyone was expecting a month ago.
Here is what happened.

Kilian Jornet: the fifth title that will have to wait

For most of the year, Kilian Jornet’s return was the headline story of the whole race.
The Spanish legend announced his comeback to Chamonix in February, four years after his last UTMB victory in 2022.
He is a four-time winner (2008, 2009, 2011 and 2022), tied with France’s François D’Haene for the outright record. A fifth title would have made him the winningest man in UTMB history.
It is not happening this year. A lingering knee issue that had already forced him out of the Western States 100 earlier this summer never fully healed, and he confirmed the withdrawal in August.
His absence lands harder because the pre-race narrative was built around him. The site had already run a full preview of his return targeting a record fifth title, a chase that now shifts to 2027 at the earliest.

What this changes at the front of the men’s race

Without Jornet, the men’s field loses its emotional centre of gravity and its most experienced pacing brain.
Every other favourite now has to build a race plan without the runner most of them would have used as a benchmark for the first 100 kilometres.

Jim Walmsley: the American who cracked UTMB, and then went quiet

Jim Walmsley is the only American man to have won UTMB, and he did it in 2023, becoming the first US winner in the race’s history.
He was expected in Chamonix, and UTMB had been briefing his return for weeks.
Like Jornet, Walmsley was forced out of Western States earlier in the summer with injury, and he never recovered enough race sharpness to justify the start line.
His absence quietly reshapes the American men’s challenge, because Walmsley was the one US name inside the top three of any credible prediction.
Without him, the highest-rated American on the 100-mile UTMB Index column is Caleb Olson at 945, followed by Ben Dhiman who leads the general Index at 946 but is only fifth on the 100-mile column.

Why this matters for the shape of the race

Walmsley’s racing style pulls the front pack forward, because he goes out fast and forces everyone else to decide whether to chase or hold back.
Without him, the opening 60 kilometres are much more likely to go conservatively.
That change of tempo helps the durability specialists, the runners who thrive when a 100-mile mountain race is settled on how well you climb at 3am rather than how fast you can run in daylight.

Tom Evans: the defending champion who never explained

Tom Evans won UTMB in 2025 and was the reigning champion.
On 13 August, two weeks before this year’s race, he announced he would not start.
He gave no reason.
That silence is unusual, because defending champions typically explain a withdrawal when the story writes itself either way, injury or otherwise.
Evans did not, and the trail running press has largely respected the choice.
The consequence is that the men’s race lines up without the runner who most recently proved he could win it.
UTMB has not seen a defending champion successfully return since Xavier Thévenard’s repeat in 2013 and 2015, so recent history was against Evans anyway, but the absence still leaves a gap at the front.

Katie Schide: the course record, the foot injury, and a race that lost its ceiling

Katie Schide’s absence is the one that reshapes the women’s race most.
Schide holds the women’s UTMB course record at 22 hours 09 minutes 31 seconds, set in 2024, a run that took more than 20 minutes off the previous mark held by Courtney Dauwalter.
Nobody else in the 2026 women’s field has run within reach of it.
She is out with a foot injury. The absence changes the maths of the race entirely, because it removes the only runner who was going to force a sub-22 hour pace on Croft and Dauwalter.

What Schide’s absence unlocks

Without the course-record holder pulling the front group along, the women’s race becomes a tactical duel between Ruth Croft and Courtney Dauwalter rather than a chase behind a runaway leader.
It also opens the podium. Names like Riley Brady (who sits second on the entry list by UTMB Index at 826), China’s Fuzhao Xiang, Nepal’s Sunmaya Budha and France’s Blandine L’Hirondel all move up a step in the projections.

The race that is left

What remains is still one of the deepest UTMB fields ever assembled, 846 elite entrants across the week, 34 more than 2025 and 46 per cent of them women.
It has a men’s Index leader (Ben Dhiman) and a women’s Index leader (Dauwalter at 859) who have never both won a UTMB before.
The betting favourites now look very different. On the men’s side, the race opens up to Vincent Bouillard (the 2024 champion who broke the 14-hour barrier at Western States this year in 13:46), Ben Dhiman, Caleb Olson and France’s Baptiste Chassagne (second in 2024 and Diagonale des Fous winner in 2025).
On the women’s side, it becomes the Ruth Croft versus Courtney Dauwalter rematch that would have been a subplot if Schide had started.
Croft is defending, and is the only woman to have won all three World Series Finals races (OCC, CCC and UTMB). Dauwalter is chasing a fourth title, having won in 2019, 2021 and 2023.
And behind them, an unknown that nobody has calibrated: Cocodona 250 champion Rachel Entrekin, racing her first UTMB.

One more thing: what the withdrawals say about ultra-running in 2026

Three of the four withdrawals (Jornet, Walmsley, Schide) are injury-related, and Evans has stayed silent. That is a signal, not a coincidence.
The world’s best trail runners are now racing more, at higher intensities, on more technical terrain than ever before. The result is a season calendar that repeatedly shows the same names appearing on withdrawal lists in August because they raced Western States or Hardrock in June or July.
The runners who make it to Chamonix healthy are, increasingly, the ones who selected carefully. That is one of the quieter storylines of UTMB 2026, and it may end up being the loudest by Sunday morning.
If you want the reasoning laid out in full, durability, not speed, is the real weapon in ultramarathons explains why.
The 100-mile UTMB starts on Friday 28 August at 17:45 CEST from Chamonix, and the official race page has the current start list, mandatory kit and cut-off times.
It will be missing four of the names most people expected to see, and it will still be one of the most important races of the year.

articles.title: There Is $10,000 Waiting in Sydney for Any Australian Who Breaks This Record
articles.description:
Most marathon prize money goes to the international elite. The TCS Sydney Marathon has built something different underneath it.

On August 30, the Australian Marathon Championships is being contested inside the race, with what organisers describe as the richest prize purse ever offered to Australian marathon athletes.

Sitting on top of that is a $10,000 bonus for any athlete who breaks the current Australian marathon records.

The Two Numbers That Matter

The marks in question are specific and, on this course, brutally demanding.

  • Men's Australian record: 2:06:22, held by Andy Buchanan
  • Women's Australian record: 2:21:34, held by Sinead Diver

Both are legitimate world-class times. Buchanan's mark would have won the Sydney Marathon outright in most years before 2024.

Why Those Records Are Hard to Beat Here

There is an obvious problem with chasing a national record in Sydney, and it is the course.

Sydney carries roughly 313 metres of cumulative elevation gain, the most of any Abbott World Marathon Major.

There is no sustained flat section longer than a few hundred metres anywhere on the route.

National records are usually set on flat, sheltered, fast courses. Athletes travel to Berlin and Valencia for exactly that reason.

Buchanan set his 2:06:22 on a fast course, not a hilly one.

Beating it in Sydney would arguably be a more impressive run than the record itself.

That tension is what makes the bonus interesting rather than routine. It is real money placed on a genuinely difficult ask.

The Man Chasing It

Andy Buchanan is the Australian record holder and an Olympian, and 2026 marks his TCS Sydney Marathon debut.

He races on home soil, in front of a home crowd, with his own record and $10,000 on the line. That is a specific kind of pressure.

He is joined by 2025 World Athletics Championships representatives Tim Vincent and Liam Boudin, plus Sydneysider Tom Do Canto, who finished second in last year's Australian Championship.

Also in the domestic men's field is Michael Roeger, the marathon world record holder in the T46 para classification.

The Women's Championship

The Australian women's race features Tokyo Olympian Ellie Pashley and Caitlin Scott, winner of the 2025 Melbourne Marathon.

Sinead Diver's 2:21:34 is a formidable target.

To put it in perspective, that time would have finished second at the 2025 Sydney Marathon behind only Sifan Hassan and Brigid Kosgei.

In 2025, the leading Australian woman in Sydney was Leanne Pompeani, seventh overall in 2:24:47. That is roughly three minutes off the national record.

Three minutes over a marathon is a lot on a flat course.

On a course with 313 metres of climbing, it is a very large gap indeed.

Why This Prize Structure Actually Matters

It is easy to read a prize purse announcement as promotional noise. In Australian distance running it is closer to infrastructure.

Australian marathoners have historically had to travel overseas to earn meaningful prize money and to race against genuinely deep fields.

Both cost money that domestic athletes often do not have.

Putting the national championships inside a World Marathon Major solves both problems in one move.

Athletes race the best in the world without leaving the country, and they compete for money that reflects the standard.

The Development Argument

Australian Athletics has framed the 2026 field as a recruitment tool as much as a competition.

The reasoning is that young Australians watching the world's best race through their own streets are the next generation of the sport.

That is not empty rhetoric. Sydney's participation has grown from around 5,300 runners in 2022 to a record 35,000 in 2026, drawn from more than 117 countries.

Visibility of that kind changes what young athletes think is possible.

The Tactical Problem for the Australians

Here is the genuine dilemma facing every Australian in the elite field on August 30.

Do you race the national championship, or do you chase the record? They are not the same race.

Racing the championship means running tactically, covering moves from your domestic rivals, and being prepared for a slow, grinding finish.

Chasing the record means locking into an even pace regardless of what anyone else does.

On a course this hilly, even pacing by the watch is close to impossible.

Effort-based pacing is the only sane approach, which makes a time-based bonus awkward to target.

The Realistic Play

The smartest approach is probably to run with the deepest possible group for as long as it lasts.

Nineteen men in the international field have run faster than the Sydney course record of 2:06:06. A capable Australian who tucks into a fast group has a legitimate chance at a personal best.

The risk is well known.

Going with a group that is running faster than your fitness allows produces a spectacular collapse after 30 kilometres, which is exactly the failure mode explored in how to run negative splits for race day success.

That decision, made in the first 10 kilometres, will determine the Australian results more than anything else on the day.

Learn More About The Method →

Limited-time reader discount available

What to Watch on Race Day

Three things worth tracking if you are following the domestic race.

The halfway split. In 2025 the men's lead group came through in 1:03:45, and any Australian near that pace is chasing something serious.

The Oxford Street climb at 15km. This is the first place a record attempt visibly falls apart, because it is early enough to feel manageable and steep enough to cost you.

Mrs Macquarie's Chair at 38 to 40km. Whoever still has functioning quadriceps on this final climb wins the Australian title, regardless of what the clock says.

The prize structure and Australian elite athlete programme are detailed by Australian Athletics, and the full confirmed field is in the official TCS Sydney Marathon announcement.

If you are running Sydney yourself rather than watching it, the taper is now the whole game, and the evidence on doing it properly is covered in taper strategy for best marathon results.

The gun goes at 6:30am. The money is real.
